investigacion.base:
I couldn't open the BEA core PCE page itself. Secondary reports of the September 30 BEA release give the latest values below. For September, most nowcasts land between 3.05% and 3.11%, which puts the outcome right on the line between rounding to **3.0** and **3.1**.

**Status quo (latest BEA release, Sep 30, 2026, August data)**
- Core PCE was up 0.2% on a monthly basis and 3% year over year, cooler than economists' expectations of 0.3% and 3.3%.
- Employ America puts the unrounded figures at +25bps month-over-month and 3.01% year-over-year.
- The annual benchmark revision lowered July's readings for headline PCE from 3.7% to 3.4% and core PCE from 3.3% to 3%. It also brought methodology changes for portfolio management, software and legal services.
- Headline PCE was 3.4%. Core PCE has stayed in a 3.0%–3.2% band since March.

**Inputs since then**
- **September CPI (Oct 14):** headline 3.7% year-over-year. Core CPI was 2.6% versus a 2.5% forecast, with core up 0.3% on the month (forecast 0.2%). Gasoline prices were 34.2% higher in September 2026 than a year earlier.
- **Nowcasts after the PPI release (~Oct 15–16):**
  - Cleveland Fed (updated 10/16): core PCE 0.28% month-over-month and 3.05% year-over-year; headline 3.60%.
  - Employ America: +34bps m/m and by −1bp to 3.09% for the y/y September core PCE reading. They flag airfares running hot.
  - Morgan Stanley: September core PCE inflation at 0.34% M/M. They also expect PPI to bring a downward revision of about -4bp to August core PCE.
  - Oxford Economics: core at 0.29% month-over-month, with year-over-year going to 3.0% (prev. 2.9%).
- **Trading Economics** projects 3.3% core by quarter-end. That looks stale compared with the nowcasts above.

**How the rounding works out**
- Starting from August's ~2.97–3.01% after revision, a September month-over-month gain of 0.28–0.34% would push year-over-year up by about 0.08–0.14 points. That's based on my rough recollection that September 2025's core monthly gain was about 0.2%; I didn't check it.
- The result would be about 3.05–3.15%, so it's close to a coin flip between 3.0 and 3.1. A 3.2 needs a hot month (≥~0.4%), and a 2.9 would need a soft print plus a larger downward revision.

**Context**
- After the Fed's September meeting, Employ America's base case is hold rates steady at the October meeting and hike at the December meeting.
- Normally core CPI runs above core PCE; the current reversed gap (2.6% vs ~3.0%) adds model uncertainty.

**Scheduled events**
- Personal Income and Outlays release on Oct 29, 8:30 a.m. ET. This is also the Q3 GDP week; I haven't seen any report of a shutdown or delay.
- The Fed's October meeting is around Oct 27–28.

**Prediction markets:** I didn't find a current Kalshi or Polymarket price for September core PCE.

**Bottom line:** The question has no Yes/No outcome; it resolves to a number. Based on current information, the most likely values are 3.0 or 3.1, with nowcasts leaning slightly toward 3.1.

**Sources:**

criterios: This question resolves to the year-over-year percent change in the Personal Consumption Expenditures (PCE) Price Index excluding food and energy ("core PCE") for September 2026, as published by the US Bureau of Economic Analysis (BEA) in the Personal Income and Outlays report scheduled for release on October 29, 2026 at 8:30 a.m. EDT. The resolution value is the figure shown for "September 2026" in the "Change From Month One Year Ago" table on the BEA core PCE page: https://www.bea.gov/data/personal-consumption-expenditures-price-index-excluding-food-and-energy — reported to one decimal place (e.g., a reading of 3.0% resolves as 3.0). Use the value as it first appears in the September 2026 release.
letra_pequena: If the October 29, 2026 release is delayed (for example, due to a government shutdown or scheduling change), the question resolves based on the first official BEA publication of the September 2026 core PCE year-over-year figure whenever it appears, with resolution waiting as needed. If the BEA permanently ceases publishing this figure, the question is annulled. Resolution is based on the originally published September 2026 figure, not on any later revision.
razonamientos:
(a) **Time left:** The release is on October 29, 2026, about 10 days away. I have seen no reports of a delay or shutdown.

(b) **If nothing changed:** Core PCE has held at 3.0% for three months, and August's unrounded figure was about 3.01%. The status quo outcome is 3.0.

(c) **If the current trend continued:** September CPI and PPI ran hot. Nowcasts put September core PCE at 0.28–0.34% month over month and roughly 3.05–3.09% year over year. That sits right on the line between 3.0 and 3.1, leaning slightly to 3.1.

(d) **Experts and markets:**
- Cleveland Fed nowcast: 3.05%.
- Employ America: 3.09%.
- Oxford Economics: 3.0%.
- Morgan Stanley: 0.34% month over month, with August revised down about 4bp.
- Trading Economics: 3.3%, which looks stale.
- I found no prediction market price.

(e) **Low scenario:** A soft September print (≤0.2% month over month, e.g. if portfolio management fees or airfares translate weakly), plus a larger downward revision to August, could give 2.9. Methodology quirks from the benchmark revision could push it lower still.

(f) **High scenario:** A hot print (≥0.4%) from financial services and airfares, or an upward revision to prior months, could give 3.2 or even 3.3.

**Distribution:** The outcome is discrete. My probabilities are roughly:
- 2.9 or lower: about 9%.
- 3.0: about 40%.
- 3.1: about 38%.
- 3.2: about 10%.
- 3.3 or higher: about 3%.

(b) **If nothing changed:** The reported rate would remain at 3.0%.  
(c) **If the recent monthly inflation pace continued:** The year-over-year rate would likely edge up to 3.1%.  
(d) **Experts and markets:** The cited nowcasts cluster around 3.0%–3.1%; the roughly 3.3% consensus estimate appears high relative to those estimates. No useful prediction-market price was found.  
(e) **Low surprise:** Softer services prices or a downward revision could produce 2.8%–2.9%.  
(f) **High surprise:** Stronger services inflation or an upward revision could produce 3.3% or more.

(a) **The time left until the outcome to the question is known:**  
10 days (scheduled for release on October 29, 2026, at 8:30 a.m. EDT).

(b) **The outcome if nothing changed:**  
Core PCE year-over-year inflation has been reported at 3.0% for three consecutive months (June, July, and August 2026); if it holds steady, the release will be 3.0%.

(c) **The outcome if the current trend continued:**  
With incoming monthly inflation indicators (September CPI core +0.3% m/m and firmer airfare/services PPI components) showing mild acceleration compared to August, continuing momentum would push the unrounded YoY rate slightly higher to round to 3.1%.

(d) **The expectations of experts and markets:**  
Post-CPI and post-PPI nowcasts cluster tightly around the rounding threshold: the Cleveland Fed projects 3.05% YoY (+0.28% MoM), Employ America projects 3.09% YoY (+0.34% MoM), Morgan Stanley estimates 3.05%–3.10% YoY, and Oxford Economics estimates 3.0% YoY (+0.29% MoM). Analysts view the rounded outcome as roughly an even split between 3.0% and 3.1%.

(e) **An unexpected scenario that results in a low outcome:**  
Downward historical revisions to July or August, combined with unexpectedly weak non-market/imputed services prices or softer healthcare provider fee reimbursements, could pull the monthly print below 0.20% MoM, yielding a YoY reading of 2.8% or 2.9%.

(f) **An unexpected scenario that results in a high outcome:**  
Substantial strength in non-CPI PCE components—particularly portfolio management fees (boosted by stock market strength), foreign travel, or hospital services—could lift core PCE to +0.40% MoM or higher, driving the annual rate to 3.2% or 3.3%.
